newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-IWS predicts significant rise in wool price.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-IWS predicts significant rise in wool price.

text.p: The International Wool Secretariat (IWS) expects a significantly higher price for wool one year from now, Chris Wilcox, the secretariat's manager information and trade policy, said on Wednesday.

"From now my guess - based on all the readings - is that prices will be significantly higher (a year from now) than today," Wilcox said at a meeting of the New South Wales Farmers' Association. He told the meeting it was highly probable that wool prices would rise to 620 cents a kg early in the new year.
IWS expects a slow and cautious recovery in wool prices, particularly after Christmas, he said.
This would follow the collapse in wool prices, from 762 cents a kg two years ago to the latest price of 557 cents, a slight recovery from the recent low point of 550 cents a kg.
"We've seen a roller-coaster ride," Wilcox said.

On the outlook for wool, Wilcox predicted that China would continue to buy from traditional suppliers, especially Australia. But there were risks in China, he said. Retail sales could go either way as the Chinese government battled inflation, but growth was still seen in the Chinese economy, he said.
The Japanese market was undergoing a recovery, with good solid demand emerging in women's wear, he said.
The U.S. market was showing continued growth, Wilcox said, but Europe was still operating on a hand to mouth basis.
Wilcox pointed to a major switch by China away from imports of wool from the former Soviet Union this year.
In the January-August period this year, China's imports of wool from the former Soviet Union dropped by 84 percent compared with the previous corresponding period, he said.
"Wool is not coming out of the (former) USSR," he said.
This followed a strong fall in stocks there and recognition by China that wool from this source was of low quality.

However, China's purchases of Australian wool in the January-August period were up by 12 percent compared with the previous corresponding period as Australia regained some of the losses of 1994 and 1995, Wilcox said.
Another encouraging sign was an early start to cold weather in Europe this year, which seemed to be lifting wool consumption already, he said.
This compared with last year's late start, when cold weather did not begin in Europe until November/December.
The price of wool was now three times that of cotton and synthetics. At this ratio wool was competitive, Wilcox said.
